CSE829 · image enhancement · domain study

Does CLALHE hold up outside the pictures it was tested on?

A published contrast-enhancement method, re-run over 146 images from five domains it was never evaluated on — chest radiographs, retinal fundus, underwater, low-light, and ordinary photographs — scored against ground truth wherever ground truth exists.

Mohammed & Isa, IEEE Access 13:62600–62632, 2025 DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3558506 5 methods × 146 images = 730 measurements

the short answer

No — and the reason is visible in the pictures

CLALHE generalises poorly. Where it appears to win, it wins on metrics that reward leaving the image alone; where ground truth exists, it is beaten by methods a decade older. On medical images it actively damages the picture.

Verdict by domain

  • Chest X-rayhurtsSeams cut across the lung fields; parameters are identical on all 40 images, so nothing adapts.
  • Retinal fundushurtsSame seams, over the retina the paper's own dataset was meant to showcase.
  • UnderwatermixedReal but small gain — and it only matches stock CLAHE, never beats it.
  • Low-lightno-opWins 0 of 15 images. Plain global HE gains 8× more against ground truth.
  • Natural photosmixedThe paper's home ground: a mild, safe enhancement, still seam-ridden as published.

Three findings carry that verdict, and each is measured rather than asserted:

  • The subimage seam is structural, not incidental. As published, CLALHE leaves a visible grid in every domain tested — 2.8× to 4.3× more visible than the image's own content. On a chest film it crosses the lungs.
  • The adaptive parameters frequently aren't adaptive. The clip limit lands on its floor of 1.0 in 73% of low-light and 55% of fundus images, and on X-rays every one of the 40 images produced identical parameters.
  • Against ground truth it loses. On low-light images global HE gains 6.5 dB where CLALHE gains 0.8 dB.

how this was measured

Setup, and one deliberate departure from the paper

Five arms were run over every image: the unmodified input as a control, global histogram equalisation, stock OpenCV CLAHE at its documented defaults (clip 2.0, 8×8 tiles), CLALHE exactly as published (CLALHE_new.py), and CLALHE with the cross-fade write-back that removes the subimage seam (CLALHE.py). All five touch only the LAB L-channel, so colour handling is identical and any difference is attributable to the luminance algorithm.

The paper scores enhancement with PSNR, entropy, AMBE, SSI, CII and RMSE, and all of those except entropy and CII compare the output to the input. That is a problem: a method that returns the image unchanged scores a perfect PSNR of ∞, a perfect SSI of 1.0 and an AMBE of 0. The metric rewards timidity, and the quieter of two enhancers wins by construction.

So two of the five domains were chosen because they ship a reference image — UIEB pairs each underwater frame with a corrected version, LOLv1 pairs each low-light frame with a normal-light capture of the same scene. There, PSNR and SSIM are measured against the reference instead, which asks whether the output moved toward a good image rather than whether it stayed near a bad one. Both scoreboards are reported throughout.

Three diagnostics were added for failure modes the global statistics miss: seam strength (the mean brightness step across the subimage grid boundaries divided by the mean step everywhere else — 1.0 means the grid is invisible), noise gain (how much louder a flat dark region got), and clipping (pixels pinned to 0 or 255).

Against the paper's published figures

The paper reports PSNR 31.822, AMBE 1.224 and RMSE 1.542 on DIARETDB1. On the fundus set here CLALHE-as-published scores PSNR 28.01, AMBE 7.98, RMSE 10.18 — the same order of magnitude on PSNR, but a much larger brightness shift. Two caveats belong with that comparison and both cut against reading it as a reproduction: the reachable archive is DIARETDB0, the sibling database from the same group and camera, not DIARETDB1 itself (the official mirror is dead); and the implementation under test clamps the clip limit to ≥ 1.0, which the paper's Eq. 3 does not. Treat the numbers below as characterising this implementation, which is the thing actually being asked about.

domain 01 · medicine

Chest X-ray: the seams land in the lung fields

hurts CLALHE as published adds a visible cross through the thorax and nothing about it adapts to the image.

Medical - chest X-ray — 40 images evaluated; one shown. Tiles are the same image through every arm.

This is the clearest failure in the study, and it is not subtle. On all 40 radiographs CLALHE derived exactly the same parameters: CBD = 4, ONS = 6, a 2×4 subimage grid, on every single image. The tile size and subdivision that Eq. 2 and Eq. 5 are supposed to adapt to image content are constant across the whole domain, because chest films all produce a similar count of histogram extrema (29–53 peaks). The “adaptive” half of the name does no work here.

What the subdivision does do is leave a seam. Measured seam strength is 4.29 against a baseline of 1.30 for the untouched film — the grid boundaries are roughly 3.3× more visible than ordinary anatomy. In the close-up below the horizontal boundary runs straight through the lung parenchyma. A radiologist reads that region for nodules and infiltrates; an algorithm that draws a brightness step across it is worse than one that does nothing.

The cross-fade variant removes the seam entirely (1.28, indistinguishable from the input's own 1.30) and is the gentler enhancement of the two, but it gains that by doing less: its CII of 1.26 trails stock CLAHE's 1.48.

domain 02 · medicine

Retinal fundus: the paper's own showcase, seamed

hurts A vertical brightness step crosses the retina; the parameters pin to a constant here too.

Medical - retinal fundus (DIARETDB1) — 40 images evaluated; one shown. Tiles are the same image through every arm.

Fundus photography is the one clinical domain the paper actually tested, so it is the fairest place to look. CLALHE lands on CBD = 4 and ONS = 6 for essentially every image (40 evaluated), producing a 2×3 grid. The seam strength of 3.95 against the input's 1.14 puts a visible vertical band across the retina — in the tile above it runs beside the optic disc.

The adaptive clip limit is also inert here: it sits on its floor of 1.0 in 55% of images for the published variant and 98% for the blended one. A clip limit of 1.0 is the weakest setting CLAHE accepts, so on most fundus images CLALHE is running a near-neutral CLAHE and calling the result adaptive.

One measurement artefact is worth naming because it would otherwise contaminate the numbers: 16% of each fundus frame is the pure-black surround outside the circular field of view. Every enhancement method lifts that surround off zero, which is invisible clinically but destroys any contrast statistic that divides by intensity. The CII here is computed only over blocks that are real image content, with the block selection taken from the input so all five arms are scored on the same pixels.

domain 03 · underwater

Underwater: a real gain, exactly equal to plain CLAHE

mixed The only domain where CLALHE clearly helps against ground truth — and it never beats the stock method it extends.

Underwater (UIEB) — 40 images evaluated; one shown. Tiles are the same image through every arm.

UIEB ships a reference image for every degraded frame, so here we can ask the question the paper's metrics cannot: did the output move toward a good image? It did. CLALHE-blended gains +0.99 dB and +0.078 SSIM over leaving the frame alone, and it improves 8 of 40 images outright.

The catch is the comparison. Stock CLAHE at its documented defaults gains +0.99 dB — the same figure to two decimals — in 4 ms against CLALHE's 217 ms, roughly 59× faster. Everything CLALHE adds — the peak/valley analysis, the CIQI search, the subdivision — buys nothing measurable over the method it is built on.

Worth noting for anyone applying this underwater: the blue-green cast is untouched. Both CLALHE implementations enhance only the LAB L-channel and leave a and b alone by construction, so colourfulness barely moves (51 in, 50 out). CLALHE is a luminance-contrast method; underwater images mostly need colour correction.

domain 04 · low light

Low-light: the domain it should own, and it wins nothing

no-op Best on the paper's metrics, last against ground truth. It wins 0 of 15 images.

Low-light (LOLv1 eval15) — 15 images evaluated; one shown. Tiles are the same image through every arm.

LOLv1 pairs each low-light frame with a normal-light capture of the same scene, which makes this the sharpest test in the study — and the result is the one that should decide the question.

Against ground truth, CLALHE gains +0.83 dB. Global histogram equalisation — the crude 1970s baseline the whole CLAHE family exists to improve on — gains +6.48 dB, about 8× more, and takes the best result on 12 of 15 images. CLALHE takes the best result on 0. Not few — none.

The picture above shows why: the output is still dark. CLALHE's clip limit collapses to its floor on 73% of these images (published variant) and 100% (blended), so it applies almost no correction to images whose entire histogram is crushed into the bottom of the range.

This is where the paper's metric choice bites. On the paper's own scoreboard CLALHE looks like the winner here: PSNR 28.3 against HE's 6.0, AMBE 8.9 against 112, RMSE 10.0 against 129. Every one of those metrics is computed between the input and the output, so a method scores well by not changing a dark image. Swap in the ground truth and the ranking inverts completely.

domain 05 · control

Natural photographs: the home ground

mixed A mild, safe enhancement — the behaviour the paper reports — with the seam still there.

Natural photos (control) — 11 images evaluated; one shown. Tiles are the same image through every arm.

Two of the paper's three datasets were consumer photographs, so this control set shows CLALHE at its best. And it does behave reasonably: a modest contrast lift (CII 1.19), a small entropy gain, brightness well preserved (AMBE 8.3 against HE's 38), and none of HE's blown highlights (0.65% of pixels clipped versus 4.7%).

This is a real strength and it is worth stating plainly: as a gentle enhancer that will not wreck a photograph, CLALHE is fine. It is just that stock CLAHE is also fine, faster, and lifts contrast further. And the published version still carries a seam strength of 4.19 here — the artifact is not domain-specific, it is structural.

cross-cutting finding 01

The seam is in the algorithm, not the images

Part 2 of the paper subdivides the image into ONS subimages, equalises each independently, and — per Section IX — merges them by concatenation. Independent histograms mean independent lookup tables, so two pixels either side of a boundary with the same input value get different output values. The result is a visible grid.

This is measurable. Seam strength compares the average brightness step across the grid boundaries with the average step everywhere else in the same image; the input's own value is the baseline, since real pictures have edges too.

CLAHECLALHE-paperCLALHE-blendedinput image (baseline)

Seam strength by domain. The dashed rule is the input image's own value — where a bar sits at the rule, the grid is invisible. CLALHE as published stands well clear of it in four of five domains; the cross-fade variant sits on it everywhere.

The fix is not exotic and does not change the algorithm: read each subimage with a margin of context and composite through a linear cross-fade whose weights sum to 1 across every boundary. The subdivision, the per-subimage histograms and the Part 1 parameters are all untouched. Its cost is that the output is slightly gentler still.

Why the paper's evaluation never caught it: PSNR, entropy, AMBE, SSI, CII and RMSE are global statistics over hundreds of thousands of pixels, and a seam is a few thousand of them. It moves the averages by almost nothing. It is only obvious when you look at the picture.

cross-cutting finding 02

The adaptive clip limit spends most of its time on the floor

CLALHE's headline contribution is choosing its own parameters: tile size from the peak count (Eq. 2), clip limit from peak and valley frequencies (Eq. 3), subdivision from the valley count (Eq. 5), with a CIQI fitness search over candidates. In practice the clip limit is pinned to its minimum of 1.0 — the weakest setting CLAHE accepts — on most images in most domains.

CLALHE-paperCLALHE-blended

Share of images where the selected clip limit lands on its floor of 1.0. On low-light and fundus images the “adaptive” parameter is effectively a constant.

The other parameters are barely more responsive. Across all 40 chest X-rays, CLALHE chose CBD = 4 and ONS = 6 — a 2×4 grid — for every single image. Across the fundus set it chose CBD = 4 and ONS = 6 for essentially all of them. Two domains with completely different content converge on the same configuration, because both produce a similar count of histogram extrema, and the count is all Eq. 2 and Eq. 5 look at.

There is a structural reason the CIQI search adds nothing, noted in the earlier audit of this implementation: maximising CIQI = (PSNR + entropy) / AMBE over the candidate clip limits is equivalent to picking the smallest one, since a weaker clip limit changes the image less, which raises PSNR and lowers AMBE together. The search reliably returns the least aggressive candidate, which is why the floor is hit so often.

cross-cutting finding 03

It cannot see 16-bit medical data at all

Everything above uses 8-bit images, because that is what is publicly downloadable. Native medical imaging is not 8-bit: DICOM radiographs and CT are stored at 12 or 16 bits, and extra range is precisely what contrast enhancement there is for.

CLALHE's parameter stage calls cv2.calcHist(…, [256], [0, 256]) and its PSNR hardcodes 255.0. Feed it the same X-ray in a 16-bit container and the histogram sees only pixels below 256:

8-bit    409600 of 409600 pixels counted  (100.0%)
16-bit    17431 of 409600 pixels counted  (  4.3%)

           n_peaks  n_valleys   CBD     I_CL   ONS
8-bit           36         35     4   3.0891     6
16-bit           0          0     8   2.0000     2

It does not raise an error. It finds zero peaks, silently falls through to hardcoded defaults, and returns an image. Every adaptive claim in the paper evaporates, and nothing in the output signals it. Native DICOM must be windowed to 8 bits first — which is itself a contrast decision, made outside the method, by someone else. The paper never states the constraint.

Reproduce with venv/bin/python -m domain_study.bitdepth_check.

what would change these conclusions

Limitations

  • The fundus set is DIARETDB0, not DIARETDB1. Same group, same camera, 130 images at 1500×1152 against the paper's 1500×1100 — a close sibling, but not the identical corpus, so the comparison with the paper's published figures is indicative rather than a reproduction.
  • CII departs from Eq. 12. The paper computes Michelson contrast over a hand-chosen ROI. With no ROI annotations across five domains it is computed densely here — every 32-pixel block as an ROI against its surrounding ring, averaged over blocks that are image content. Applied identically to all arms, so the ratio stays fair, but the absolute values are not the paper's.
  • Sample sizes are modest — 40 images per domain, 15 for low-light (all of LOLv1's eval set), 11 natural photographs. Enough to establish the parameter-collapse and seam findings, which are near-universal within each domain; thinner for the reference-based margins.
  • Only two implementations were tested, both from this repository. Differences from the authors' own code — the clip-limit clamp at 1.0 and the histogram smoothing before peak detection are two known ones — would shift the numbers, though not the seam, which follows from the published Part 2 directly.
  • No satellite or remote-sensing domain. It was scoped out of this run; the 16-bit finding above is the part of that domain's answer that generalises, since most usable satellite imagery is 12- or 16-bit.

reproducing this

Everything here regenerates from four commands

Sources are public and non-gated; the image subset is chosen with a fixed seed, and reruns are byte-identical apart from timings.

venv/bin/python -m domain_study.datasets --all      # ~350 MB, 5 domains
venv/bin/python -m domain_study.run_study           # raw_results.csv + summary.csv
venv/bin/python -m domain_study.make_figures        # comparison tiles
venv/bin/python -m domain_study.report              # this page

Per-image measurements live in results/raw_results.csv (730 rows), domain means in results/summary.csv.
